messages.subject: Asymmetric component in bilat.symmetry
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

I'm working with geometric morphometric analysis of symmetry of skull data. Dealing with bilat.symmetry() I have found the following issue when we have object symmetry. The function computes asymmetric component by subtracting symmetric component from the first n landmark configurations of the dataset (where n is the number of specimens). It is OK when there are only one replicate per specimen. But when there are several replicates we can get problems when replicates are follow one by one (eg, 1 1 2 2 3 3 etc). In my opinion, in the case of multiple replicates asymmetric component should be computed as differece between average of replicates and symmetric component.
This is not a great issue because there are no such problems with matching symmetry and DA- and FA-components of asymmetry. But I spent a bunch of time this week disentangling algorithmic details of implementation.
Specifically, I discuss lines 285-286 of the bilat.symmetry.r file:
>     asymm.component <-simplify2array(lapply(1:n.ind, function(j)
>     {mn.shape + A[,,j] - symm.component[,,j]}))

Best regards,
Basil Yakimov,
Lobachevski State University of Nizhni Novgorod

messages.subject: Plotting of two block PLS (two.b.pls())
messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph R group,

I am quantifying the evolutionary shape changes of the skull and vertebral column of the salamandrid genus Lissotriton. I assessed the covariation between the skull shape and the first trunk vertebrae by a two block partial least squares analysis. I want to create a ggplot2-plot from the elements produced by the two.b.pls function, as i managed to do so for PCA, PTA and phylomorphospace plots. However I have a hard time figuring out which elements from the two.b.pls output are accessible for ggplot2. Could anyone tell me which elements should be used by ggplot2 and how they have to be constructed in order to produce a plot?

Thanks in advance and best regards,

Stefan

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] accounting for evolutionary allometry in shape evolution study
messages.body_plain:
Nick,

The answer here is ‘it depends.’ If by downstream phylogenetic comparative methods (PCM) you mean multivariate PGLS - as found in say, ‘procD.pgls’ in geomorph or the ‘lm.rrpp’ function in RRPP (implemented as GLS) – then one may simply consider including size as an additional covariate. There is no restriction on that.

On the other hand, if you meant some other multivariate PCM, such as evaluating phylogenetic signal or evolutionary rates, that would require a bit more thought on your system, and what aspects of trait variation you wish to capture in your analysis.

Dean

To my best understanding, both approaches can be used to establish patterns of direction and magnitude of shape change with size by testing for differences in slope angle and length, but they visualise different aspects of the results where HOS visualise them in size-shape space and PTA in morphospace.

Thank you for your given time and effort.

Sincerely,

Igor

messages.body_plain:
Dear Basil, and others,

I wish to respond to your inquiry.  The bilat.symmetry function did indeed have some legacy code that did not make sense.  We had code for computing the difference between subjects, averaged over replicates - as you intuited - but only applied it to matching symmetry (and it eludes us why or how we missed it on object symmetry).  The fix was simple - just had to remove the condition for matching or object symmetry (which only implicates the set-up for the shape analyses, but not the analyses, themselves); however, we wanted to test the function a bit before sending the updates to our stable version of the software on GIthub.  We have done that now - sorry for the delay and inconvenience.

Thanks for bringing the issue to our attention!

Mike

> On Feb 1, 2019, at 1:34 AM, Василий Якимов <basil....@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Dear colleagues,
>
> I'm working with geometric morphometric analysis of symmetry of skull data. Dealing with bilat.symmetry() I have found the following issue when we have object symmetry. The function computes asymmetric component by subtracting symmetric component from the first n landmark configurations of the dataset (where n is the number of specimens). It is OK when there are only one replicate per specimen. But when there are several replicates we can get problems when replicates are follow one by one (eg, 1 1 2 2 3 3 etc). In my opinion, in the case of multiple replicates asymmetric component should be computed as differece between average of replicates and symmetric component.
> This is not a great issue because there are no such problems with matching symmetry and DA- and FA-components of asymmetry. But I spent a bunch of time this week disentangling algorithmic details of implementation.
> Specifically, I discuss lines 285-286 of the bilat.symmetry.r file:
> >     asymm.component <-simplify2array(lapply(1:n.ind, function(j)
> >     {mn.shape + A[,,j] - symm.component[,,j]}))

Ani,

By just looking at the code, it seems you switched the order of the data and the tree, as per the physignal help file. "physignal(A, phy, iter = 999...)", where A is the data, and phy is the phylogeny.
If the arguments are not specified, they must be entered in the same order as in the documentation.

The following lines of code are equivalent and should both work and give the same result.
species.ps <http://species.ps/> = physignal(species.means, must.tree.matched, iter = 10000, seed = NULL, print.progress = TRUE)
species.ps <http://species.ps/> = physignal(phy = must.tree.matched, A = species.means, iter = 10000, seed = NULL, print.progress = TRUE)

You can also leave out arguments if you do not change the default to get the same answer as the 2 lines above.
species.ps <http://species.ps/> = physignal(species.means, must.tree.matched, iter = 10000)

Hope that works for you!
Bryan

messages.subject_clean: minimum sample size for modularity test using CR?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to identify changes in patterns of cranial modularity between age classes of different mammal species, but for some (e.g. extinct species), I have really small sample sizes for each class ranging from 1 to 9 individuals, while others are a bit better (up to 16). Basically it's just hard to get a hold of young specimens for CT scanning since most of these are threatened or endangered.

I was wondering what the minimum reasonable number of specimens would be for the modularity test in geomorph. I read in Adams 2016 (Evaluating modularity in morphometric data: challenges with the RV coefficient and a new test measure. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 7, 565–572), that the CR coefficient still performs well at low sample size, where it's estimated for simulated data sets with 5 to 500 specimens.

I'm just curious if the values I get will be difficult to confidently interpret, or if I should rather try to combine classes into larger categories. The ones I have are based on tooth eruption.

Thanks for any advice,
Christy

Christy,

I believe for modularity, the number of variables is more compelling than the number of specimens.  You can have three specimens and if there is high modularity, you will detect it.

The other side of the coin - in my opinion - is using a lot of variables, especially if Procrustes residuals, might yield higher modularity because landmarks in close proximity will be inherently more correlated and modules are normally defined by landmarks in close proximity.  If one floods the analysis with many landmarks, I’m not sure “significant” modularity is anything for which to marvel.  More research is needed in this regard, but concerning your question, I would not worry about small sample sizes compared to other analyses where the number of subjects, rather than the number of variables, is more limiting.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Christy,

I believe you have mis-interpreted Adams 2016. In that paper I demonstrated that the expected CR test measure estimated from data remains stable across differing sample sizes;  as opposed to the RV coefficient, whose expected value changes with both N and p.  However, I did not demonstrate that significance tests perform well at low sample sizes (recall that parameter estimation and statistical evaluation are two different steps of every hypothesis-testing procedure).

To my knowledge, the type I error and power have not been investigated for any modularity method (CR, RV, or EMMLI) when N << p. At first glance one might suspect some issues in these cases. For instance, one is estimating more variance/covariance components than one has specimens, so the covariance matrix is singular. This means that parametric methods using likelihood and inverse-based approaches will not work. However, the CR is not implemented in that manner, either for estimation or statistical evaluation. Nonetheless, a thorough investigation of its type I error and other properties when N << p has not been fully investigated.

Curiously, as I’ve been typing this I did perform a very quick type I error evaluation under N=5, and p=60, and type I error was reasonable (~0.06). However, this is just an initial investigation of such properties. I for one would want to do considerably more theoretical investigation before I convinced myself that the CR, or any modularity measure and subsequent test, performs well in cases where N <<p.

Hope this helps!

Dean

library(geomorph)

N = 5

p = 60

dat <- lapply (1:1000, function(j) matrix(rnorm(N*p), nrow=N, ncol=p))

res <- lapply(1:1000, function(j) modularity.test(dat[[j]],partition.gp <http://partition.gp> = gl(2,30),print.progress = FALSE))

p.res <- unlist(lapply(1:1000, function(j) res[[j]]$P.value))

length(which(p.res<=0.05)) / 1000

Nicole,

To expand on Dean’s reply, a ~ Csize + species model would be a common slopes model allowing for different group intercepts (means) and a ~ Csize model would be both a common slope and common intercept model.  Your full model, ~ Csize * species, will find unique intercepts and slopes for species.  Therefore, you might want to think about exactly what the hypothesis is that you wish to test and what the best null model should be.  The HOS test in procD.allmoetry used the former null model (different intercepts, common slope), so if you are trying to mimic that, you probably should use that as a null model in advanced.procD.lm.

Mike

messages.subject_clean: log size transformation in allometry tests - necessary?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm embarrassed to ask this question, so please forgive me if it's too simple.

I'm wondering what is the significance of log-transforming size in allometry tests, for example using procD.lm and procD.allometry.

For all of these tests I have multiple groups (species), and they have significantly different ontogenetic allometries. So far I have been running all tests using a skull length measurement instead of centroid size, because it's easier to directly relate the points in the output graphs to specimens in my sample, which is important for describing when during growth certain changes occur, e.g., after weaning or tooth eruption.

Log-transforming size doesn't change the results much, but it does change the graphical outputs, for example when plotting CAC on skull length vs log-skull length. I understand the value of log transformation in linear regression and to visualize equal units of change along the x-axis, but I'm not sure it's necessary for these types of tests. My skull lengths range from ~8-242 mm.

Thanks for any advice on this,
Christy

Hi Christy,

I don't think this question is basic or simple at all, actually it is a very good one!

Generally, log-transformation will bring your data closer to normality, and also make variation relative to the scale of the trait, which (at least for me) helps interpretation, especially when looking at different groups, which might have different ranges and variances. But I am not surprised your results do not change much with and without logs for CS (or, put another way, if that where the case I would tend to think more about statistical or sample artifacts, rather than a biologically interpretable pattern).

Hope this helps

One could also argue that there is a biological reasoning rather than a statistical one.  Many morphological and physiological attribute scale exponentially with size (e.g., mass and metabolic rate), especially if such attributes tend to correspond more so with volume or surface area, rather than linear distance (as how size was classically measured). I have often wondered if centroid size, although univariate, behaves more like a volume than a linear distance with its correlation of shape. One could probably confirm this with simulations - I have not bothered.  Anyway, because log transformation converts an exponential relationship to a linear one - which is helpful for least-squares based statistics - the biological and statistical reasons for doing it are in concert. However, I think doing this with centroid size is a relic from days when size was measured as a linear distance, and because it does not impose a problem (I think) it just sort of sticks around as convention.

A good policy is to address the distribution of residuals and use a transformation (or not) based on the their best “behavior” (tending toward multivariate normality and homoscedasticty).

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your answers. So it sounds like it's not necessarily wrong to use the true size value in allometry tests, but that log-transforming can make interpretation easier.

Regarding normality, I looked at both the size and log-size variables and neither are normally distributed (this is for the entire dataset, not within species). I also checked the residuals from a regression of shape on size, and those are (at least checking several of them separately, although I didn't do this in a multivariate sense). When I run the allometry tests with and without log-transforming, the R2 is slightly higher for true size but the F and Z values are slightly lower. Again, none of this actually changes the overall interpretation of the results so I feel it's more an aesthetic issue at this point regarding graphics. I do see how log-size on the x-axis makes it easier to see species differences (mine range from mouse-size to wolf-size), but it just means I have to backtrack to the true value to get to the actual specimen and developmental stage.

I don't mean to beleaguer the point, but as Mike points out, it seems to be a standard regarding centroid size so I wasn't sure about other (linear) variables.

I'm happy for any more input, and thanks again for your feedback.

Christy

Alicia,

Two things. First, it’s a bad idea to call an object the same name as a function. The function, data, and your name of data means R has to discern between the two, which can cause errors. Second, you do not name the data within the data frame. Therefore, it is no longer a set (a matrix) but instead, the variables in the original set are liberated. For example, if you have a matrix of three variables, called “dat”, comprising x, y, and z, in the defining of the data frame, you need to say,

dat = dat

To not do that - like you did - is tantamount to telling R you want to add x, y, and z, separately.

Hope that helps.
Mike
